did_you_know.text: Did you know? According to the chapter, after Rehoboam’s kingdom was firmly established, he and all Israel abandoned the law of the LORD; the chapter presents this departure from the law as a turning point in his reign.
Did you know? In the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign, Shishak king of Egypt marched against Jerusalem, and the text connects the invasion with Judah and Israel’s unfaithfulness to the LORD.
Did you know? Shishak’s army is described as including 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and a vast host from Egypt—Libyans, Sukkites, and Cushites.
Did you know? Shishak captured the fortified cities of Judah and reached Jerusalem, but the chapter does not describe the city as being completely conquered.
Did you know? The prophet Shemaiah told Rehoboam and the leaders of Judah that the invasion was the result of abandoning the LORD: “You have abandoned me; therefore I have abandoned you to Shishak.”
Did you know? Rehoboam and the leaders of Israel humbled themselves and said, “The LORD is righteous”—an acknowledgment of the justice of the judgment following the prophet’s message.

Did you know? When the LORD saw that they had humbled themselves, he announced that he would not destroy Jerusalem completely, but would grant them “some measure of deliverance” and restrain his anger.
Did you know? Shishak took the treasures of the LORD’s temple and the treasures of the royal palace, including the gold shields Solomon had made.
Did you know? Rehoboam made bronze shields to replace the gold shields and entrusted them to the commanders of the royal guard, who guarded the entrance to the king’s palace.
Did you know? Although Rehoboam grew strong and reigned in Jerusalem for seventeen years, the chapter’s conclusion states that he did evil because he had not set his heart on seeking the LORD.
